Text:
A neonate's body weight follows a predictable course:

At birth: {{c1::6 to 8 lb (3 to 3.5 kg)}}

First week: falls {{c1::5% to 10%}} from fluid loss

Second week onward: gains about {{c1::1 ounce (30 g) per day}}

Doubles birth weight by {{c1::4 to 6 months}}

Triples birth weight by {{c1::1 year}}
Back Extra:
Ex: a 7 lb newborn is about 14 lb at 6 months and about 21 lb at 1 year.

Pitfall: doubling and tripling are multiples of the birth weight, not of whatever the infant weighs at the time.

Text: A neonate's head accounts for about {{c1::25%}} of total body weight, which is why neonates and infants tend to land {{c2::headfirst}} when they fall.
Back Extra:
Why: the risk of head injury is compounded by an infant's inability to extend the arms to cushion or slow a fall.

Pitfall: keep head and spinal trauma high on the index of suspicion after any fall by a neonate or infant.

Text: Neonates are primarily {{c1::nose::nose or mouth}} breathers, and infants younger than {{c2::6 months::age}} are especially susceptible to congestion that can lead to viral upper respiratory infections.
Back Extra:
Distinguish: the nose-breathing rule is stated for the neonate (0 to 1 month), while the heightened susceptibility to nasal congestion runs through the first 6 months.

Why: an infant who breathes through the nose has no easy second route, so even mucus can compromise ventilation.

Text: You are dispatched for a 2-month-old who is reportedly choking. The mouth and throat are clear, yet the infant is still struggling to breathe, so you check next for obstruction of {{c1::the nasal passages::anatomic site}}.
Back Extra:
Why: neonates and young infants breathe primarily through the nose, so mucus alone can present as a choking emergency.

Pitfall: susceptibility to nasal congestion runs through the first 6 months, so a reported choking in this age group is often a blocked nose.

Text:
Airway obstruction is more common in infants than in older children and adults. Compared with an adult, what is anatomically different about an infant's airway and head?

{{c1::a larger tongue relative to the size of the oral cavity}}

{{c1::a proportionally shorter and narrower airway}}

{{c1::a proportionally oversized occiput}}

{{c1::a more flexible trachea}}
Back Extra:
Cue: name what is bigger (the tongue and the occiput), what is smaller (the airway), and what is floppier (the trachea).

Why: the oversized occiput, the flexible trachea, and an infant's limited ability to reposition are why the EMT must protect airway patency through proper positioning.

Text: In an infant, the EMT preserves airway patency through proper positioning, because both {{c1::hyperextending}} and {{c1::hyperflexing}} the head and neck can easily produce an airway obstruction.
Back Extra:
Meaning: hyperextension tips the head too far back, and hyperflexion lets the chin drop toward the chest.

Why: an infant has limited or absent ability to reposition, so whatever head and neck position the EMT sets is the one the infant stays in.

Text: An infant's rib cage is {{c1::less::more or less}} rigid and the ribs sit {{c1::horizontally::orientation}}, which explains the {{c2::diaphragmatic (belly) breathing}} typically seen in infants.
Back Extra: Pitfall: belly breathing is the normal pattern for an infant, so abdominal movement by itself is not a sign of distress.

Text: {{c1::Barotrauma}} is {{c2::pressure-induced trauma to the lungs}}, and in an infant the cause is {{c3::forceful ventilations and overinflation}} with a bag-mask.
Back Extra:
Why: an infant's lungs are fragile, the breathing muscles are immature, and the alveoli are relatively few.

Pitfall: an infant's oxygen need is low but a stressed infant compensates poorly, so extra force adds risk without adding benefit.
